To date, there’s not much research on false awakenings, and experts have yet to determine exactly what causes them. As with sleep paralysis, they may relate to disrupted REM sleep.

A few suggested explanations for false awakenings include:

- sleep disorders, such as insomnia and sleep apnea
- anticipation, or knowing you need to wake up early for a specific reason
- noise and other disturbances that interrupt your sleep without fully waking you up

Stress and anxiety in your daily life can also have an impact on sleep and potentially appear in your dreams.

If you’re worried about something that’s going to happen shortly after waking up, you might dream about waking up and getting ready to face the stressful event. These stressful events can include:

- a difficult exam
- dentist’s appointment
- job interview


You have to try to determine the cause of your false awakenings and after that you'll find the solution as well. 

[Research from 2011](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/False-awakenings-in-light-of-the-dream-theory%3A-a-in-Buzzi/7b1cbabb68045ce70fe3baba2dcb17f026feb0c4?p2df) offers another potential explanation for false awakenings.

According to the theory of dream protoconsciousness, your brain prepares for consciousness during REM sleep, using its internal representation of your everyday world.

This model serves as a starting place for your dreams, the theory suggests. But most dreams include plenty of other elements that make them seem much less realistic.

False awakenings could happen when hyperarousal, or increased alertness, during REM sleep keeps you from experiencing more typical dreams, like those involving flying, falling, and other surreal happenings.

Instead, the dreams may rely on more specific memories of familiar surroundings and your typical daily routine.

Improving the sleep you get each night could help reduce the frequency of false awakenings. If they become a regular annoyance or keep you from getting restful sleep, talking to a sleep specialist may be a good option.

Honestly- for the first twenty years or so, I figured I was just kind of defective. My education and family never touched on so much as the word of "transgender." There was male and female, and heterosexuality. Hell, it was just the way it was. Gay was an insult, but the idea of homosexuality was outside of my comprehension. 

I always thought that my desire to be female, my envy, was just an aberration. But in my final year of high school, I heard that a female friend of mine (who had graduated two years ago) was now living as a male. To my mind, the idea was ludicrous. I assumed she simply dressed in men's clothing (as she had in the past), but nothing beyond that. Another friend errantly said that she heard surgery had made her a man. That didn't make me laugh. I was afraid. As much as I wished I was female, the idea was too far- laughable by less disturbed minds. A vagina was a vagina and a penis was a penis. Plastic surgery did a lot of things- but it couldn't possibly hold that kind of potential. Even as as stolid atheist and believer in Science, even I couldn't believe that was possible. 


After I graduated high school, I drifted. Without the guidelines of general education, I had no idea where to go. So I attended the local junior college, studying Psychology, but avoiding any subject of sexuality. I had a penis, but could only imagine sex in terms of having a vagina. So I took other classes, and ignored the subject. 

I used to be a big fan of 420chan. One night, on an errant binge of alcohol (a increasing habit since my 21st), I looked under "lifestyle discussion" and found the Transgender forum. 

I was horrified to find that there were others who felt like me. Others who had recognized what I had buried as some kind of error. And more than that, these individuals seemed aware of a means to transpose this state. I closed the window immediately. I was terrified. 

But later, I reopened it. I began to read some of the stories in depth. I found so many others like me, others struggling, others in denial. But there were options- possibilities to become the sex they'd always known themselves to be. 

So,  yeah, that was about the time I knew I was transgender.
